asof: Quotes captured live intraday Wed Sep 2, 2026 (~11:20 AM ET), so both the Sep 1 selloff and today's partial rebound are in the price columns. Macro chips update automatically from FRED with a lag.

nextCpi.label: Next CPI print
nextCpi.delta: August data, and it is suddenly the most important print of the year. Warsh all but said at Jackson Hole that a hike is on the table if inflation does not improve, so this number decides whether the Sep 15-16 meeting is a hold or the first hike of his tenure. July came in at 3.3% headline and 2.5% core, cooling for a third straight month; the new complication is oil, up 5% on the Iran strikes.

nextFomc.label: Next FOMC
nextFomc.delta: A live meeting in the fullest sense: after Warsh's hawkish Jackson Hole speech (inflation 'work to do', openly keeping a hike on the table), futures-market odds of a September hike jumped to roughly 57% from 35% the day before. The 2-year yield rose 12 basis points on the speech alone. A hike would be the first since 2023 and would pressure every long-duration growth name on this board.

top_picks.name: Vanguard S&P 500 ETF
top_picks.thesis: You like ETFs because you own the whole field without betting the farm on one company, and the last two weeks made the case again. VOO holds the 500 largest US companies for a rock-bottom 0.03% fee. It closed Friday at 703.71, about 1.5% off its record, 1.8% above its 50-day average and up 3.7% over 30 days, with just 3 distribution days in the trailing window against 5 to 6 for the semiconductor and Nasdaq funds. Underneath, the week split hard: chips fell about 5% on rising Treasury yields while healthcare, uranium and the quantum names ran. Owning all 500 turned that tug-of-war into a mild -1.4% week and a still-rising 30-day trend.
top_picks.why_now: September opened with the index at the bottom of its 30-day range ($761.78 to $777.88 on SPY) on normal volume: 2 distribution days, no heavy-liquidation events. A hawkish Fed and an oil shock are exactly the conditions dollar-cost averaging exists for; this week's scheduled buy lands about 2% below the Aug 28 high. It is the first trading week of a new month and the pick was reviewed: it stays.
top_picks.risk: A September hike (futures now price roughly 57% odds) plus an escalating Iran conflict could extend the drawdown well past the 30-day range; the 10-year at 4.81% intraday is the highest since 2023 and a push toward 5% would re-rate the whole index lower. That changes the entry price, not the 10-year case.
sources: Stock market today: Dow, S&P 500, Nasdaq rise after July jobs report surprises to the downside
Treasury yields drop after surprise jobs loss in July

grade.note: Held at A, and Friday strengthened rather than merely maintained the case. One distribution day is the cleanest flow reading anywhere on this board, and it was earned during a week when the semiconductor funds accumulated seven each. The index absorbed a 3.8% drop in Western Digital to a 30-day low and turned in a record close. Best Sharpe of the three picks at plain market risk (0.65), lowest historical drawdown (-32.1%), a 13.5% ten-year compound return, and roughly 23% odds of a down year. The standing caveat keeps it from being anything other than a schedule holding: 100% of its 30-day range is the worst entry point in a month, so keep buying on a calendar rather than in one lump.

top_picks.bear_case: The bear case is that you are buying the AI capital-spending cycle at its peak without realising it, because the index label hides the concentration. Roughly $725 billion of hyperscaler capital spending in 2026 is holding up a large share of index earnings, that figure is up about 77% year over year, and a growing portion of it is debt financed rather than funded from cash flow. If capital spending plans are trimmed even modestly, the earnings estimates underneath a third of this index move with them. Add a hot CPI print forcing a September hike and you have both the numerator and the denominator working against you at a record high.

competitors.name: VTI
competitors.note: The near-identical sibling: total US market at the same 0.03% fee, adding mid and small caps for a little more diversification. It rose 0.71% on Friday to a 30-day high and carries two distribution days to VOO's one. A coin-flip alternative.

competitors.name: SPY / IVV / SPLG
competitors.note: The same S&P 500 index. SPY is the most liquid (best if you ever use options) but costs 0.09%, while IVV and SPLG match VOO on cost. SPY carried three distribution days to VOO's one on Friday, which is a quirk of how the share classes trade rather than a difference in what you own.

competitors.name: SCHD
competitors.note: The defensive alternative: a dividend-value basket with far less technology concentration, more income and a lower expected long-run return. It was the best 30-day performer among the core funds at up 5.08% and closed at a 30-day high. A complement to VOO rather than a replacement.

top_picks.factors: Quality and breadth. This is the only holding on the shortlist where you are not making a sector bet, and the flow data says institutions agree: one distribution day, zero heavy liquidation events, and no heavy liquidation events across any of the 21 funds on the ETF shelf. The 30-day range position of 100% is the one factor arguing for patience.
top_picks.trade_reasoning: Treat the levels below as a discipline for sizing, not a trading plan. The reference entry is Friday's 710.71 close, which is a poor opportunistic price and a perfectly ordinary scheduled one. The volatility-based stop near 620.56 is roughly 12.7% lower, which is useful mainly as a reminder of how much ordinary noise this fund produces in a normal year rather than as an instruction to sell. Monte Carlo puts one-year odds of a loss at about 23% with a median gain near 14%, which is the honest shape of buying a broad index at a high: usually fine, occasionally uncomfortable, rarely permanent.

top_picks.name: Eli Lilly
top_picks.thesis: The reason this sits at number two is that it is the one holding on the shortlist whose fortunes have almost nothing to do with AI capital spending. Lilly closed at 1,185.71 on Friday, down 0.52% on a day when 57 of 70 names rose, which tells you exactly what it is: the ballast. The business case rests on the two GLP-1 franchises, which grew 91% and 123% in the most recent quarter and drove revenue up 48%, with full-year guidance raised to $85 billion to $87 billion. US market share widened to 60.9% against Novo Nordisk's 38.8% after Novo's CagriSema lost a head-to-head trial. The quant history is the strongest of the three: a 31.1% ten-year compound return, a Sharpe of 0.94, and the best reward-to-risk setup on the shortlist at 3.71.
top_picks.why_now: The defensive rotation this pick was built for is happening: XLV is at 70% of its 30-day range (+5.8% on the month) while growth ETFs sit at 0%, Merck is +17% on the month, and Lilly holds above $1,170 with a steady bid. Earnings that do not depend on a 2030 buildout are what the market pays for at a 4.8% 10-year. Reviewed at the month turn: it stays.
top_picks.risk: Six distribution days, the most of any pick, show institutions trimming into strength; the Medicare drug-pricing negotiation remains the structural overhang, and a resolution of the rate scare would rotate money back out of defensives as fast as it rotated in.
sources: CMS Issues First Proposed Rule for IRA Medicare Drug Price Negotiation
Key Facts About Medicare Drug Price Negotiation

grade.note: Held at A. Friday added no new information, which for this holding is the point: it closed down 0.52% while the speculative end of the board rose 8% to 15%, and that non-participation is precisely the diversification you are paying for. The flow reading is unremarkable in a good way, at 67% of its 30-day range, 2.4% above its 50-day and four distribution days. What keeps it from displacing VOO at the top is not the business, which is excellent, but the combination of a premium multiple and a live regulatory process with a firm date on it. Comments close Aug 17.

top_picks.bear_case: The bear case is that the GLP-1 franchise is priced as though it compounds at this rate indefinitely, and two things could break that. First, price rather than volume: Medicare negotiation, expanding international reimbursement scrutiny and eventual biosimilar entry all push realised price per patient down even as prescriptions rise. Second, the competitive respite may be temporary; Novo losing one head-to-head trial does not remove a well-capitalised competitor, and an oral GLP-1 from any credible entrant would reset expectations quickly. At this multiple, merely good growth is not enough.

competitors.name: Novo Nordisk (NVO)
competitors.note: The direct competitor and the contrarian option. It rose 2.81% on Friday but sits at just 41% of its 30-day range with a heavy liquidation flag in the trailing window, so it is genuinely washed out in a way Lilly is not. You would be buying the loser of the CagriSema head-to-head trial at a discount.

competitors.name: AbbVie (ABBV) / Merck (MRK)
competitors.note: The lower-multiple, higher-yield alternatives if the GLP-1 valuation is the sticking point. AbbVie closed at just 11% of its 30-day range, among the cheapest readings on the whole board, though it sits 2.03% above its 50-day so the trend is intact.

competitors.name: XLV
competitors.note: The diversified way to own the sector without adjudicating which drug wins. It closed at 82% of its 30-day range, 4.96% above its 50-day with four distribution days, and it materially reduces the single-name policy risk that the Aug 17 CMS comment deadline creates.

top_picks.factors: Quality and growth at a full price. The strongest fundamentals on the shortlist and the best reward-to-risk ratio in the quant work (3.71), offset by the fullest valuation. The flow factors are neutral, which is exactly what you want in the position meant to behave differently from everything else you own.
top_picks.trade_reasoning: The reference entry is Friday's 1,185.71 close. The volatility-based stop near 992.03 is about 16.3% lower, which is a fair description of how much this stock moves on a single trial result or policy headline, and the take-profit near 1,903.91 produces the best reward-to-risk on the shortlist at 3.71. Monte Carlo puts one-year odds of a loss at about 18.8%, the lowest of the three, with a median gain near 31.2%. The practical approach is to scale in rather than buy at once, and to treat the Aug 17 comment deadline as a likely source of a cheaper print rather than a reason to avoid the name.

top_picks.name: VanEck Semiconductor ETF
top_picks.thesis: This is the diversified way to own the AI hardware layer without picking which chip company wins. It closed at 582.70 on Friday, up 1.96%, and the case for owning the basket rather than the parts has now been demonstrated three sessions running from three different directions: it lost only 1.04% while AMD fell 7%, gained about 1% while Western Digital fell 11%, and on Friday rose 1.96% while Western Digital fell another 3.8% to a 30-day low. The fund is doing exactly what a basket is supposed to do. The underlying demand is not in question: roughly $725 billion of hyperscaler capital spending in 2026, up about 77% year over year, with Microsoft disclosing an $80 billion Azure order backlog it cannot fill because of power constraints.
top_picks.why_now: The thesis strengthened while the price went nowhere: Nvidia beat and raised, then announced a program to mobilize $500 billion of institutional capital for the AI buildout, and memory (Micron +12.5%, SanDisk +19% on the month) confirms real demand. SMH sits about 5.7% below its 50-day average at the bottom of its 30-day range on quiet volume. For a multi-year holder that is a better entry, not a worse story. Reviewed at the month turn: it stays, with the scale-in unchanged.
top_picks.risk: Rates, not demand: at a 4.8% 10-year the market pays less for 2030 earnings, and a September hike would likely push SMH through the bottom of its range. Concentration risk is unchanged (Nvidia and TSMC dominate the fund), and the photonics carnage (Credo -18% today) shows how fast the high-multiple end reprices.
sources: Big Tech AI spending plans reach $725 billion
Western Digital Sinks 16%, SanDisk Falls 11%, Micron Drops 6% as Memory Selloff Hits Storage Stocks

grade.note: Upgraded from B- to B, on measured improvement rather than on Friday's price. Two of the three things holding the grade down have moved: distribution days fell from nine to seven, and the distance below the 50-day average narrowed from 4.4% to 2.06%. The fund also absorbed a third consecutive single-name blow-up without breaking, which is the basket earning its fee. What still caps it at B rather than B+ is that it remains below its 50-day, seven distribution days is still the joint-highest cluster on the board alongside SOXX, and Friday's gain came on roughly half of normal volume. Keep scaling in on weakness rather than chasing strength.

top_picks.bear_case: The bear case is a memory-led inventory correction that spreads. SanDisk was up 469% and Western Digital 202% year to date before their reports, and both were sold on guidance despite beating, which is the classic signature of a cycle where the good news is already in the price. If NAND and DRAM pricing rolls over, the earnings that justify the whole group's multiple roll with it. The second leg of the bear case is financing: about a third of the $725 billion of hyperscaler capital spending is now debt funded, and the credit market has started charging more for it. Demand does not have to fall for the trade to unwind, only the cost of funding it has to rise.

competitors.name: SOXX
competitors.note: The direct iShares alternative and currently the weaker of the two: 67% of its 30-day range against SMH's 73%, 4.1% below its 50-day against 2.06%, and thinner volume at 0.48 times average. Same idea, slightly worse readings on every flow measure.

competitors.name: VGT
competitors.note: The broader technology fund, which dilutes the memory cycle risk that is currently doing the damage. It closed at a 30-day high, up 1.55%, but carries eight distribution days, the highest count on the entire ETF shelf, so institutions have been selling it steadily.

competitors.name: ARTY / SEMI
competitors.note: The AI-thematic alternatives, both with cleaner flow readings at three distribution days each. ARTY closed at 96% of its 30-day range and SEMI at 94%. Useful if you want the theme with less concentration in the pure semiconductor cycle.

The flow factors are the constraint: seven distribution days, still below the 50-day average, and half-normal volume on the up days. Improving, not yet healthy.

Take-profit near 950.33 gives a 2.54 reward-to-risk. Monte Carlo puts one-year odds of a loss at 17.1%, the lowest of the three, with a median gain near 33.8%, but note the fifth-percentile outcome of -18.3% is the fat tail you are accepting. Scale in on weakness.

top_picks_note: September rotation review: it is the first trading week of a new month, which is when these three are eligible to change. All three were kept. The regime shifted hawkish, and this trio was built for exactly that mix: the whole market at a discount (VOO), the defensive sleeve that leads in a rate scare (LLY), and the AI demand story at a technical discount (SMH). Grades, bear cases, and quant workups below update from this decision. Research, not financial advice.

insights.title: The pullback is real but orderly: SPY sits at the bottom of its 30-day range with no panic selling
insights.body: Since the last briefing the market absorbed three shocks: a hawkish Warsh at Jackson Hole (Aug 28), US strikes on Iran (Sep 1, Dow down more than 400 points, S&P -0.71%, Nasdaq -1.03%), and a 10-year Treasury that touched 4.81% this morning, its highest since November 2023. Yet the tape shows repositioning, not liquidation. SPY is at 0% of its 30-day range ($761.78 to $777.88) but carries only 2 distribution days, zero heavy-liquidation events, and a volume ratio of 1.06, which is normal turnover. The heavy-volume selling is concentrated where you would expect in a rate scare: speculative nuclear (OKLO, SMR, LEU all logged a heavy down day), quantum (QBTS -17% on the month), and high-beta small caps (Russell 2000 -1.2% today while the Dow rose). Nvidia logged 2 heavy-volume down days but ended the month up 5.2% and is +4.2% today: that is profit-taking after a beat, not distribution.
insights.matters: For a long-term holder this is the difference between trimming and panicking. The index selling is shallow and low-conviction; the froth is what is being sold. Scheduled buys of VOO and SPY land near the bottom of the monthly range this week. The speculative sheet (Sheet 2) is where the real drawdowns are, and chasing it before the 10-year stabilizes is the one clear mistake on offer.
sources: Motley Fool: Sep 1 slide and oil surge

insights.title: Warsh put a hike on the table at Jackson Hole, and the bond market believed him
insights.body: Warsh's first Jackson Hole address as Fed chair (Aug 28) was deliberately hawkish: inflation remains above target, the Fed has 'work to do', and he came as close as a chair ever does to signaling a rate hike if the data does not improve. The 2-year yield jumped more than 12 basis points to 4.36% on the speech and September hike odds rose to roughly 57% from 35%. Then the Iran strikes added an oil shock on top: crude up 5% Monday, and the 10-year closed Aug 31 at 4.75% before touching 4.81% intraday today, the highest since November 2023. The 30-year sits above 5.2%. For the first time in this cycle, the realistic near-term path for rates is up, not down.
insights.matters: The 10-year near 4.8% is the single biggest counterweight to every valuation on this board. It compresses the multiple the market will pay for long-duration growth (semis, quantum, space, small nuclear) and raises the bar for the AI capex trade. It also makes boring cash flow more valuable: the dividend and value sleeves (SCHD, the utilities inside the nuclear majors, healthcare) are doing their job this week. Do not restructure a long-term plan around one meeting, but expect chop into Sep 10 CPI and the Sep 15-16 FOMC.

insights.title: US strikes on Iran: oil up 5%, and an energy shock is the worst kind of inflation for this Fed
insights.body: The US launched new strikes on Iran ahead of Monday's session, sending crude up 5% and Treasury yields higher across the curve. The equity damage was concentrated in high-beta: the low-volatility sleeve of the S&P fell just 0.2% Monday while the high-beta sleeve dropped 2.1%. Today the market is attempting to stabilize (Dow +0.4%, S&P roughly flat) on hopes this is escalate-to-de-escalate, but oil in the high $80s feeds directly into the headline CPI print Warsh just tied his hike decision to. Steel and domestic industrials caught a bid (Nucor +3.2% today), and defense-adjacent names held up.
insights.matters: Two board effects. First, an oil-driven CPI surprise on Sep 10 is now the clearest path to a September hike, which would hit the speculative sheet hardest. Second, sustained high energy prices strengthen the long-term nuclear and grid case (CEG, VST, GEV, ETN, PWR): expensive hydrocarbons are the best marketing clean baseload power ever gets. A long-term holder does not trade headlines, but this is the risk column of the thesis flashing, not the reward column.
sources: Motley Fool: stocks slide, oil surges on US-Iran tension

insights.title: Nvidia is mobilizing $500 billion of other people's money, and that is the Capital battlefield going live
insights.body: The week's most important AI-infrastructure story was not a chip: Nvidia announced a partnership with six large asset managers to mobilize more than $500 billion in third-party capital for the AI buildout, and the stock is up 4.2% today on the follow-through, reclaiming $226 after closing August up 5.2%. This is the answer to the question hanging over the whole trade since credit spreads started widening: who funds the next wave of data centers if the hyperscalers slow down? The design is to move AI infrastructure financing off hyperscaler balance sheets and into institutional capital, exactly the business BlackRock, KKR, Apollo, and Blue Owl on this board exist to do.
insights.matters: This de-risks the demand side of the thesis (funded buildout continues even if one hyperscaler blinks) and directly feeds the AI Capital & Financiers sector on Sheet 1. It also supports the picks: SMH's largest holding just underwrote the financing of its own demand. The caveat: leverage-funded buildout at a 4.8% 10-year is exactly how credit-cycle risk enters the story, which is why the credit-spread metric in the thesis scorecard stays red.
sources: Yahoo: Sep 2 session and Nvidia capital program

insights.title: The nuclear majors delivered real numbers this week, while the rate scare punished the speculative end
insights.body: Fundamentals in the power trade keep improving: Constellation raised its 2026 EPS guidance to $11.50 to $12.50, and Talen cleared more than 10 gigawatts in the PJM capacity auction, worth up to $2.2 billion, yet TLN is still down almost 15% on the month because capacity-auction winners trade like leveraged bonds when the 10-year spikes. Uranium spot has settled in the mid $80s per pound with Citi projecting $100 to $125 into year-end on a structural deficit (2025 production about 173M pounds vs 204M pounds of demand). URA is +7.7% on the month but has cooled to 25% of its 30-day range with one heavy-liquidation day, and the small developers were hit harder: OKLO, SMR, and LEU each logged a heavy down day in the last week.
insights.matters: The long-term power thesis is getting stronger while its stock prices consolidate: guidance up, capacity prices up, fuel in deficit, and an oil shock reminding everyone why baseload matters. For a buy-and-hold investor the mature end (CEG, the utilities, URA/NLR for the basket) is behaving fine; the developer end (OKLO, SMR, NNE) is a rate-sensitive venture bet and is being repriced as one. Size it accordingly.
sources: Yahoo: nuclear stocks and the AI power boom

insights.title: Memory quietly became the strongest group on the board: SanDisk +19%, Micron +12.5%, SMCI +28% in a month
insights.body: While attention was on Nvidia, the memory and storage sector finished the month as Sheet 1's best performer: SanDisk +19.3%, Micron +12.5% (now near $944 after its run), and Super Micro +28.2% on the servers side. HBM and enterprise storage supply remain tight, and the AI buildout's appetite for both is the reason. The photonics group gave back its August leadership in ugly fashion: Credo fell 18% today on heavy volume, and Fabrinet, Astera Labs, and Ciena are all down double digits over the month. High-multiple optical names are the most rate-sensitive corner of the AI supply chain, and it shows.
insights.matters: The board's positioning columns earn their keep here: memory's gains came on real accumulation while photonics is flashing distribution (Credo's drop came with 4 distribution days and a heavy-liquidation event). For long-term exposure, the memory theme is investable through MU, SNDK, and SOXX; the photonics names are the ones to watch for a washed-out entry rather than to chase on strength.

insights.title: The defensive rotation is visible: healthcare is the best-positioned section on the board
insights.body: XLV sits at 70% of its 30-day range, up 5.8% on the month, while nearly every growth-facing ETF on the shelf sits at 0% of its range. Merck is +17.3% over the month, Novo Nordisk +3.3% today, and Lilly is holding above $1,170 with a quiet bid. This is what a rate-and-oil scare does: money that will not leave the market moves to earnings that do not depend on a 2030 buildout. The caution flag is Lilly's 6 distribution days, the most of any pick, which says some institutions are trimming into strength even as the sector leads.
insights.matters: This validates the LLY pick's role in the Top 3: it is the sleeve that works when the 10-year is at 4.8%. The Medicare drug-pricing negotiation remains the sector's real long-term risk, worth more attention than any one week of trading. If the Fed does hike on Sep 16, expect this rotation to extend.

smart_money.intro: Timing context, not buy signals. What the flow data says about who is selling this dip and who is leaning into it.

items.title: Goldman's book came into this shock at record gross leverage, and that is the fragility to watch
items.body: Goldman's prime brokerage data shows gross leverage entered the fall at record highs for a third straight year with net leverage near 3-year highs, and allocator surveys show a record 45% (net) plan to add hedge fund exposure in 2026. Translation: the professional community was positioned long and levered when Warsh turned hawkish and the Iran strikes hit. Today's tape has the classic de-grossing signature: the Russell 2000 down 1.2% while the Dow rises, and the heaviest selling in crowded high-beta names (Palantir -5.3% today after a +43% month). When leverage comes down, the most crowded longs fall hardest regardless of fundamentals. A signal about flows, not a verdict on the companies.
items.matters: Record leverage means the fast money is fully invested and extended: good for the tape while it works, and the fuel for sharp de-grossing if Nvidia or Jackson Hole disappoints. For a long-term holder the read is simple: do not be the one buying what leveraged funds are forced to sell in a de-gross, which is why the chip pullback is a scale-in, not a lump sum.

items.title: Fresh data at last: fast money bought volatility protection and deepened its index shorts into the rally
items.body: The CFTC positioning table below updates from the weekly Traders in Financial Futures file; the latest week still reflects positioning set before the Jackson Hole speech and the Iran strikes, so read it as the starting point of this repricing rather than the reaction to it. Coming into the shock, fast money had been adding volatility protection while asset managers stayed heavily net long equities. The next release shows whether the levered community actually de-grossed or just hedged.
items.matters: The timing is the whole point. This snapshot is dated Tuesday Aug 4, three days before the jobs report and the record close, so it shows professionals hedging into strength rather than reacting to weakness. That combination (deeper index shorts, a flip to long volatility, and long-only managers quietly trimming) is what caution looks like in positioning data, and it sat directly underneath the best week since April. Two honest caveats. First, leveraged funds are frequently wrong and their index shorts are often hedges against long cash equity rather than outright bearish bets. Second, this data is four days stale and Friday may have forced some of those shorts to cover, which would itself explain part of the move. The practical takeaway for a long-term investor is narrow: professionals were paying up for insurance ahead of Aug 12 while the index made a record. That is a reason to keep purchases scheduled and modest, not a reason to sell anything.
sources: CFTC Traders in Financial Futures, report dated Aug 4, 2026

items.title: The capex floor is now $710 billion plus, and Nvidia just added a $500 billion financing lane beside it
items.body: Microsoft, Meta, Amazon, and Alphabet are collectively guiding to more than $710 billion of combined 2026 capex, and McKinsey sizes the global AI data-center buildout near $7 trillion by 2030. On top of that, Nvidia's new program with six large asset managers aims to mobilize over $500 billion of third-party institutional capital, moving part of the buildout off hyperscaler balance sheets entirely. The demand signal for everything on Sheet 1, from semis through electricals to power, remains the strongest fact in the entire thesis. The late-October Q3 guidance updates are still the confirm-or-cut moment.
items.matters: This is the number that decides whether the entire first sheet of this board is a durable investment or a cycle, and it is the reason the least glamorous layers are often the safest way in. Microsoft's $80 billion power-constrained backlog is the single most useful sentence in this section, because it says the bottleneck has moved from chips to electricity. That is a direct argument for the power section that the market spent Friday liquidating, and the divergence between the two is the clearest mismatch on the board right now. The practical takeaway: the demand evidence supports owning the picks-and-shovels layers (semiconductors through SMH, electrical and conduit, and the regulated power majors) rather than the speculative end. Watch the financing side as the thing that would change the thesis. Demand does not have to fall for this trade to unwind, only the cost of borrowing to fund it has to rise.
sources: Big Tech AI spending plans reach $725 billion
Hyperscalers Hit $700 Billion in 2026 AI Spending Plans

items.title: Two government decisions are actively moving prices on this board, and both have dates attached
items.body: The first is trade policy in optical networking. A draft US proposal would restrict imports of new Chinese optical transceivers, and the FCC is preparing to enact a ban on new Chinese transceiver models. That single draft rule is a large part of why Coherent rose 41% in a week and why Applied Optoelectronics gained 9.19% on 2.44 times average volume on Friday. It has repriced the same handful of stocks in both directions repeatedly this summer as the draft has advanced and stalled. The second is healthcare pricing. Public comments on the CMS proposed rule for Medicare drug price negotiation close on Aug 17, with the final rule expected in the autumn, and the proposed changes specifically target high-expenditure biologics, fixed-combination products and products that previously qualified for the small biotech exception. Separately, the GOV badges on this board mark names where the US government either holds equity (Intel, MP Materials, Lithium Americas) or is the anchor customer (Centrus, BWX, Rocket Lab, Palantir), and four of those seven rose more than 7% on Friday.
items.matters: Policy-driven moves deserve a different treatment from demand-driven ones, and mixing them up is one of the more expensive mistakes available to a long-term investor. A draft rule can be softened, delayed or reversed, so any price move that depends on it should be treated as reversible until the rule is final. That argues for patience with the photonics names at 30-day highs, and it argues for using the Aug 17 healthcare deadline as a shopping window rather than a reason to avoid the sector. The GOV badges cut both ways too: government backing lowers the risk of a company running out of money and raises the risk that its fortunes turn on an election or an appropriation. The practical takeaway: when a position on this board moves on a policy headline, ask whether the underlying demand changed. On Friday, in photonics, it did not.
sources: Coherent Corp. jumps 41% over the week as China optics restrictions coincide with earnings report
Key Facts About Medicare Drug Price Negotiation

primer.intro: A large AI data center is a machine built in physical layers, and money flows into it from the top (the customers who order it) down through every supplier who makes a piece. Here is where the dollars land, and why the least glamorous layers can be the safest way to invest.

sections.h: Start at the top: the customers
sections.p: The hyperscalers (Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Oracle) announce the giant spending budgets, now roughly $725B in 2026, that everyone else competes to capture. Owning them is the most diversified way to own the theme, because their core businesses (ads, cloud, software) fund the AI bet and keep earning even if AI spending pauses. Two cautions: the market now scrutinizes the return on that capex, and roughly a third of it is now funded with debt rather than cash flow, which hands the bond market a vote it did not previously have. Meta's latest raise was attributed to higher component prices rather than more capacity, which is a cost increase dressed as an investment increase.

Nvidia (NVDA) designs the GPUs that do the AI math; AMD (AMD) is the challenger; Broadcom (AVGO) builds the custom chips hyperscalers increasingly design in-house, a trend now challenging Nvidia's near-monopoly. None own factories: TSMC (TSM) prints the chips using machines only ASML (ASML) makes, and every GPU needs memory from Micron (MU). Highest growth, highest risk, and the layer that falls first on any overcapacity or competition scare. It is also now the layer priced for perfection: AMD grew data-center revenue 107% and the stock still fell 7%.

Memory deserves its own line. Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron control over 95% of global DRAM and have shifted a large majority of combined output to high-bandwidth memory for AI accelerators. That has sent AI memory pricing sharply higher and left consumer-grade memory scarce, which is a margin tailwind for MU, SNDK and WDC and a cost shock for every device maker. It makes this the most cyclical layer of the buildout, and the most crowded: about 16% of Goldman's prime-brokerage exposure was tied to AI memory names as of June 30, which is why guidance misses here move the whole group violently. The live fundamental question is efficiency: compression techniques that shrink the memory footprint of AI models could either soften the shortage or, by making inference cheaper, spread AI workloads widely enough to increase memory demand overall. SK Hynix is Seoul-listed, so US investors reach it mainly through the baskets.

sections.h: Layer 2: The box and the room
sections.p: The chips get assembled into servers by Super Micro (SMCI) and Dell (DELL). A rack of AI chips runs blazing hot, so it needs advanced cooling and power distribution from Vertiv (VRT), and fast switches from Arista (ANET) to connect racks together. This is the guts of the room, and these are project businesses whose revenue lands unevenly quarter to quarter, which is why single-day moves of 5% or more are routine here in both directions.

AI splits one job across thousands of chips, so they must talk at the speed of light over fiber. Transceivers and lasers come from Coherent (COHR) and Lumentum (LITE), contract manufacturing from Fabrinet (FN), long-haul interconnect from Ciena (CIEN), and the actual glass fiber from Corning (GLW). Optics content rises with every hardware generation as 800G gives way to 1.6T. This layer is now also a policy battleground, with a draft US rule targeting Chinese-made optical modules that has sent the group up 21%, down 2% and up 3% in four sessions without the rule itself changing at all.

The least glamorous and often most attractive layer: switchgear from Eaton (ETN) and Hubbell (HUBB), the steel and PVC conduit that carries every wire from Atkore (ATKR), jobsite supply from WESCO (WCC), transmission and substation build from Quanta (PWR), and the raw steel from Nucor (NUE). Physical, hard-to-substitute, multi-year backlogs. Four of these six names are sitting at or near the very top of their 30-day ranges, which is what sustained accumulation looks like.

A data center is useless without electricity, and AI has made power the true bottleneck. Existing-reactor operators signing long deals are Constellation (CEG), Vistra (VST) and Talen (TLN); the regulated fleet owners are Dominion (D), Southern (SO), PSEG (PEG) and Entergy (ETR); fuel comes from Cameco (CCJ) and Centrus (LEU); reactor and SMR technology from BWX (BWXT), Oklo (OKLO) and NuScale (SMR); and near-term gas-turbine and grid power from GE Vernova (GEV). Because the regulated names are effectively bond proxies, this layer trades against the 10-year yield as much as against the AI story, which is why it has been the weakest part of Sheet 1 while yields climbed.

Follow a dollar of capex: it lands most heavily on the chip layer, which captures the most dollars but carries the most risk (a rival can win a socket, custom silicon can erode the moat, and an overcapacity or return-on-investment scare hits it first). The power, conduit, cooling and fiber layers are lower-binary: whatever chip and model win, the building still needs steel, copper, transformers and megawatts. A newer distinction sits alongside that one: how the buyer is financed. Suppliers paid by hyperscalers with real cash flow are on firmer ground than pure-plays that borrow to buy chips, which is why the neoclouds trade on credit spreads rather than on demand.

macro_strategy.regime_label: Regime shift: the market repriced from rate-cut hopes to a live September hike, with an oil shock on top
macro_strategy.regime_detail: Three forces converged in five sessions. First, Warsh used his debut Jackson Hole address to put a hike openly on the table, and futures odds of a September hike jumped to roughly 57% from 35%; the 2-year rose 12 basis points on the speech. Second, US strikes on Iran sent crude up 5% and pushed the 10-year from 4.67% to 4.75%, with a 4.81% intraday print today, the highest since November 2023. Third, the equity reaction has been a rotation rather than a rout: SPY fell to the bottom of its 30-day range on normal volume, high-beta and speculative names took the real damage (Russell 2000 -1.2% today, quantum -17% on the month for QBTS, the small nuclear developers logging heavy-volume down days), while healthcare, dividend value, and the megacap AI names with real earnings held or rallied (Nvidia +4.2% today on its $500 billion capital program). The quant model still reads an uptrend, but the leadership underneath it has rotated defensively. The next ten days decide the regime: CPI on roughly Sep 10, then the FOMC Sep 15-16.

drivers.reading: His debut Jackson Hole speech put a rate hike openly on the table and tied it to the inflation data. Futures odds of a September hike jumped to roughly 57% from 35%; the 2-year rose 12 basis points on the speech alone.
drivers.playbook: Expect chop into the Sep 10 CPI and the Sep 15-16 FOMC. Keep scheduled buys running; hold new discretionary money for the other side of those two dates, or lean it defensive (VOO, LLY, SCHD-style exposure).

drivers.reading: US strikes on Iran sent crude up 5% and yields higher; energy inflation lands directly on the CPI print the Fed chair is watching. High-beta took the damage (the S&P's high-beta sleeve fell 2.1% Monday vs 0.2% for low-vol).
drivers.playbook: Do not trade the headlines. Note the second-order effect: expensive hydrocarbons strengthen the long-term nuclear and grid case (CEG, VST, GEV, ETN, PWR), which is already the best-performing thesis on the board.

drivers.reading: Highest since November 2023. This is the discount rate on every long-duration growth story on the board, and the reason SMH, quantum, space, and the small nuclear developers all sit at the bottom of their ranges while healthcare and dividend value lead.
drivers.playbook: Above 4.8% and rising favors cash flow over promises: the defensive sleeve earns its slot. A retreat toward 4.5% is the all-clear that historically re-rates the growth complex fastest.

drivers.driver: AI capex plus Nvidia's capital program
drivers.reading: The bull anchor is intact and broadening: $710B+ of combined 2026 hyperscaler capex guidance, and Nvidia is mobilizing over $500B of third-party institutional capital so the buildout no longer rides only on hyperscaler balance sheets.
drivers.playbook: This is why the dip in the AI complex is a repricing, not a thesis break. SMH below its 50-day with demand confirmed is the quality dip; the read-through names are BLK, KKR, APO, and OWL on the financing side.

scenarios.trigger: Sep 10 CPI cools despite oil, Iran de-escalates
scenarios.response: The hike odds collapse, yields ease off 4.8%, and the defensive rotation reverses. The AI complex resumes leadership with the capex and capital-program news as fuel; this week was the buyable reset.

scenarios.trigger: CPI runs warm and the Fed hikes Sep 16
scenarios.response: First hike of the Warsh era. Growth multiples compress, the speculative sheet takes the worst of it, and healthcare, dividend value, and mature power extend their lead. Long-term plans survive fine; new money favors VOO, LLY, and cash-flow utilities until the curve stabilizes.

scenarios.trigger: Oil keeps climbing into a hiking Fed
scenarios.response: The stagflation-lite tail. Hard assets, energy, and uranium hold up; nearly everything else re-rates lower. Low probability, but it is why the risk monitor keeps the 10-year and credit spreads red and why position sizing on Sheet 2 stays small.

macro_strategy.positioning: No panic and no heroics. Scheduled long-term buys continue and land near the bottom of the index's monthly range. New discretionary money leans to the defensive and cash-flow end (VOO, LLY, SCHD-style exposure, mature nuclear) until the CPI-FOMC sequence resolves. Do not add to Sheet 2 speculatives while the 10-year is making new highs; the heavy-volume selling is concentrated exactly there. If the bull scenario plays out, SMH below its 50-day with an intact demand story is the highest-quality dip on the board.

watchlist_notes: Refreshed intraday Wed Sep 2 after four sessions of regime shift: Warsh hawkish at Jackson Hole, US strikes on Iran, the 10-year at 4.81% intraday. Month-turn movers: Palantir +43% over 30 days but -5.3% today as crowded longs de-gross; Super Micro +28%, MP +22.6%, SanDisk +19%, Merck +17%, Micron +12.5% on the month. Damage list: TSSI -26.7%, QBTS -17.2%, Applied Materials and Talen both about -15%, and Credo -18% today alone on heavy volume. AST SpaceMobile is +9.8% today against a -12% month. Heavy-liquidation flags currently sit on OKLO, SMR, LEU, QBTS, CRDO, and DELL; Nvidia's two heavy down days read as post-earnings profit-taking, with the stock +4.2% today on the $500B capital program.

thesis.objective: own the enablers of the AI supercycle and the next era of abundance

metrics.label: Hyperscaler AI CapEx
metrics.delta: 2026 combined guidance, MSFT + META + AMZN + GOOGL
metrics.note: Plus Nvidia's new $500B third-party capital program: the buildout's funding base is broadening beyond hyperscaler balance sheets.

metrics.label: Data-center power demand
metrics.delta: CEG guidance raised; TLN cleared 10GW at PJM
metrics.note: Capacity auctions keep clearing at records; an oil shock only strengthens the clean-baseload argument.

metrics.label: Uranium spot
metrics.note: Structural deficit intact (about 173M lb production vs 204M lb demand in 2025); price consolidating after the summer run.

metrics.label: GPU / accelerator supply
metrics.delta: NVDA guided Q3 to $107-108B vs $104B consensus
metrics.note: Demand confirmed by the beat-and-raise; memory (HBM) tightness now showing up in MU and SNDK prices.

metrics.label: AI-infra credit spreads
metrics.note: The $500B third-party capital program is also $500B of credit exposure; this is where a funding crack would show first.

metrics.label: 10Y Treasury
metrics.note: Warsh has a hike on the table; the discount rate on every long-duration story on this board.

risks: A September Fed hike (futures near 57% odds): multiple compression across every long-duration growth name
Iran escalation sustains the oil spike, feeding CPI and forcing the Fed's hand while hitting consumer demand
Power shortages slow AI deployment (grid interconnect queues, transformer lead times)
Capital markets tighten: AI-infra credit spreads are widening while the buildout leans harder on borrowed money
Hyperscaler capex guidance gets cut (the single number holding up the entire thesis; next read late October)
Semiconductor supply chain disruption or Taiwan escalation
watchlist: Sep 10 (approx) August CPI: Warsh tied the hike decision to it, and the oil spike lands right on it
Sep 15-16 FOMC: first live-hike meeting of the Warsh Fed; watch the 2-year and hike odds into it
Iran: escalate-to-de-escalate or a sustained conflict; crude in the high $80s is the tell to watch
Nvidia's $500B third-party capital program: which six asset managers, what structures, how fast it deploys (BLK, KKR, APO, OWL read-through)
Whether SMH holds the bottom of its 30-day range and reclaims its 50-day; memory strength (MU, SNDK) says demand is fine
Hyperscaler Q3 capex guidance (late Oct): confirm or cut
